The dumplings were clearly handmade, with wrappers thin enough to see the filling through but sturdy enough to hold together perfectly on the cart ride to our table. We tried the har gow, siu mai, and char siu bao, and every single one was fresh, flavorful, and served piping hot. The service was fast and attentive, with carts circulating frequently so we never had to wait long for our next dish. Prices were very reasonable for the quality and portion sizes, and the space itself felt lively without being overwhelming, even on a busy weekend morning. This is now our go-to spot for dim sum, and I'll be recommending it to everyone I know. Five stars, no notes!

plain: Bistro the cat had never left the apartment building, but on the night the fire escape window blew open, curiosity won. He slipped onto the ledge and discovered a whole world humming below: alleyways glowing with neon signs, a fish stall abandoned for the night with irresistible smells drifting up, and a fearless pigeon flock that scattered the moment he appeared. Bistro chased shadows across three rooftops, tumbled into a stack of cardboard boxes outside a bakery, and nearly got adopted by a kind-hearted street vendor who mistook him for a stray. By dawn, smelling faintly of fish, he found his way back up the fire escape, slipping through the window just as his owner woke up, none the wiser about the wild night behind her sleepy cat's contented purring.

plain: Start with three days a week of full-body strength training using simple, low-skill movements: bodyweight squats, push-ups (knee variation if needed), rows using a resistance band or dumbbell, and planks, doing 2-3 sets of 8-12 reps each. Add 20-30 minutes of low-impact cardio, like brisk walking, on two or three other days to build baseline endurance without overwhelming your joints. Since you sit all day, prioritize hip flexor and chest stretches, along with some basic mobility work for your upper back, to counteract the effects of prolonged sitting. Keep sessions to 30-45 minutes so the habit feels sustainable rather than exhausting, and increase difficulty gradually every couple of weeks. Consistency matters far more than intensity when you're just starting out.
